messages.subject_clean: multivariate analysis with percentages as dependent variable
messages.body_plain:
dear all,

I apologize in advance for my ignorance, I know my request sounds trivial to most of you.

Participants in an online survey chose one among five possible reactions relative to a refusal to an invitation

Participants have different L1s and the percentages reflecting their choices are aligned like in the Excel example attached.

The main research question is: which differences among percentages are significant? Authors of this survey want to know if and where the L1s impact learners' choices.

Is there a model (a guess that a model is needed, am I right?) that computes multiple chi-square and that makes a post-hoc comparison (similar to Tukey) among percentages?

Thank you so much for helping on this

Stefano

messages.subject_clean: multivariate analysis with percentages as dependent variable
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stefano,

It appears that there are only 3 possible responses in your table, whereas you say there are 5 in your mail (maybe because the table is an example).

Let me paraphrase your questions and let me know if it matches perfectly what you want to find out.

1) Is the difference in percentages significantly different between the reactions and the different speakers?

2) Does L1 have an impact on learners' choices? (difficult to answer because we cannot speak of cause-effect relationship here, but of correlation)

Since you just have different L1s as one categorical dependent variable and different reactions as one independent categorical variable, why "multiple" chi-squared test? Moreover, cf. Gries' warning (2013: 190): "Again: never ever compute a chi-squared test on percentages - always on 'real' observed frequencies!"

Best,

C.B.

messages.subject: Re: [StatForLing with R] Re: multivariate analysis with percentages as dependent variable
messages.subject_clean: [StatForLing with R] Re: multivariate analysis with percentages as dependent variable
messages.body_plain:
I would recommend a multinomial regression since percentages usually
don't meet the assumptions that at least parametric tests (and the
desired post-hoc tests) have; while transformations such as arcsine
and logit might help, why not deal with the dependent variable as what
it is - categorical - and if you use a multinomial regression, you
have access to all the arsenal of contrasts and general linear
hypothesis tests (all the stuff I'd love to deal with in SFLWR, the
hypothetical 3rd ed. ;-) ) to find out whatever you want:

###########################
rm(list=ls(all=TRUE)); set.seed(1)
library(car); library(effects); library(nnet)

RESPONSE <- factor(c(rep(c("compliance", "delay", "denial"), c(46, 100, 54)),
                     rep(c("compliance", "delay", "denial"), c(30, 90, 80)),
                     rep(c("compliance", "delay", "denial"), c(40, 100, 60))))
L1 <- factor(rep(c("english", "french", "german"), each=200))
summary(x <- data.frame(RESPONSE, L1))
# this simulates your data set with a sample size of 200

prop.table(table(L1, RESPONSE), 1)
# checking

model <- multinom(RESPONSE ~ L1)
Anova(model, type="II") # p of L1 = 0.04488
summary(model, Wald=TRUE)
confint(model)

plot(allEffects(model), ylim=c(0, 1), type="probability", grid=TRUE)
###########################

Best,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries
----------------------------------
Univ. of California, Santa Barbara
http://tinyurl.com/stgries
----------------------------------
